item.title: Watch as OutKick's Trey Wallace braves Hurricane Isaias' before Alabama-Georgia showdown in Tuscaloosa
item.description: Trump's attendance was halted and kickoff conditions shifted as Hurricane Isaias bears down on the Alabama-Georgia game at Bryant-Denny Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
Hurricane Isaias has made landfall near the Florida Gulf Coast, and it has directly affected several college football games with some kickoff-time changes and even a cancellation.

The storm isn't stopping No. 6 Alabama from hosting No. 2 Georgia on Saturday night, but make no mistake that the on-field play could certainly look different than originally anticipated.

For starters, ESPN's "College GameDay" was forced to move indoors because of the storm that is slowly making its way toward the Atlantic Coast . School officials also halted any sort of tailgating until noon local time.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The storm also halted President Donald Trump from attending the highly anticipated SEC bout.

Both Georgia and Alabama rank quite well in the rushing attack - the Bulldogs' 198.3 rushing yards per game rank 28th in the country, while Alabama is 10 spots below at 186.4. That comes on 34.3 and 38.4 rushing attempts, respectively (Georgia is 81st there, but the Tide are 38th).

HURRICANE ISAIAS FORCES NUMEROUS COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES TO HAVE CHANGES, INCLUDING A CANCELLATION

If the rain holds steady, it could affect the passing attack, which is already not necessarily a strong suit for either program. Alabama throws the ball 27.2 times a game (99th), while Georgia is 105th in the country with 26.3 passes per contest.

The rain is expected to stop by kickoff, but not after nearly 24 hours of it, which may have turned the grass surface of Saban Field at Bryant-Denny Stadium into a swamp (it is equipped with quite the advanced draining system).

Both teams enter the game at 5-0, and it is the ninth time since the 2018 national championship in which both squads are ranked inside the top 10 in the nation.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

It is a massive SEC showdown that will set the tone for both teams moving forward this season, with Alabama hoping to make a statement about where it stands right now during the Kalen DeBoer era, while Kirby Smart hopes to start adding wins against the Tide in regular-season play.

OutKick's Trey Wallace contributed to this report.

item.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital, returned to prison after botched execution, attorneys say
item.description: Christa Pike is back at prison after surviving a botched lethal injection, but her attorneys say she still struggles with arm injuries and memory problems.
item.content:encoded:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital and returned to prison after surviving a botched lethal injection that left her with serious medical complications, her attorneys announced.

Pike, who survived two doses of the execution drug pentobarbital on Sept. 30, is back at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years, according to a joint statement from her legal team.

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," the statement read. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."

CHRISTA PIKE NOW CONSCIOUS AND TALKING AFTER SURVIVING 2 DOSES OF LETHAL INJECTION DRUG

The statement was issued by attorneys Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen of Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason of the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender.

The attorneys did not disclose when Pike was discharged or whether she has recovered from complications they previously described, including pneumonia, a blood clot and injuries to her arms.

Ferrell told BBC Radio 4 on Thursday that Pike had begun walking around her hospital room but continued to struggle with injuries to her arms and memory problems.

CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEY SAYS SHE'S 'UP AND WALKING' MORE THAN A WEEK AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION

"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much," Ferrell said. "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."

Pike's recovery comes after her attorneys said they believed she was brain dead Monday evening before she unexpectedly regained consciousness the following morning.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville.

LETHAL INJECTION SURVIVOR CHRISTA PIKE'S FORMER SATANIST BOYFRIEND COULD BE RELEASED IN 5 YEARS

The failed execution has prompted legal action, with a Tennessee judge ordering the state Department of Correction to preserve physical and electronic evidence related to the execution attempt.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has halted executions for the remainder of 2026. It remains unclear whether or when the state will seek to carry out Pike's death sentence.

Fox News Digital's Mike Ruiz contributed to this report.

item.title: Ron DeSantis deploys an army of linemen as Florida races to clear roads, restore power after Isaias' landfall
item.description: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis deployed 16,000 linemen and pre-dawn road crews across the state as officials warn of post-storm hazards from Isaias.
item.content:encoded:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis deployed state crews early Saturday to clear major highways and bridges after Isaias made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane, but former FEMA Administrator Craig Fugate warned that deadly dangers can persist long after the hurricane passes.

Hurricane Isaias made landfall along the Florida Panhandle late Friday, leaving hundreds of thousands of people without power as intense winds continued across the Southeast. FOX Weather reported four storm-related deaths across Florida and Alabama.

Despite the widespread outages, DeSantis said crews made early progress clearing major roads and restoring power.

EXCLUSIVE: WOMAN WHO STOLE $1.7M MEANT FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS GETS PRISON TIME AS DHS CRACKS DOWN ON FEMA FRAUD

HURRICANE ISAIAS THREATENS GEORGIA VS. ALABAMA SEC SHOWDOWN AS TRUMP PLANS TUSCALOOSA VISIT

"We scrambled assets at 0300 for road clearing and also for search and rescue, should that have been needed. Fortunately, we have not gotten requests for our search and rescue assets. I think that's cautiously a good sign," DeSantis told "Fox & Friends Weekend."

"We have had people clearing the key arteries like Interstate 10 and the key bridges from when it was pitch black at three or four in the morning. And they're [going to] continue to do that," he added.

The governor said Florida had positioned 16,000 utility workers ahead of landfall to speed up power restoration and reduce the risk of prolonged outages.

"I'd much rather have that than let the storm go by and say, 'Oh, well, we need 10,000 linemen. Let's see if they can get here by Monday morning,'" DeSantis said.

DEM GOV LASHES OUT AS TRUMP HUD SCRUTINIZES NEARLY $2B IN DISASTER FUNDS OVER FRAUD CONCERNS

"So the more you can stabilize everything, and yes, of course, the search and rescue when that's needed is very, very important. But when you do that, then you create stability in the situation, and then we can work if someone's home got damaged, if someone needs something, and we can fulfill those requests," he added.

DeSantis said wind shear weakened Isaias before landfall, limiting the extent of structural damage unlike Hurricane Michael, which devastated Panhandle communities in 2018.

DHS FIRES 3 MORE FEMA WORKERS AFTER IG REPORT FINDS CREW SKIPPED HOMES WITH PRO-TRUMP SIGNS

FOX Weather reported wind gusts exceeding 110 mph but said conditions before landfall helped prevent "an even more catastrophic scenario along the Florida Panhandle."

Fugate warned that cleanup efforts pose additional risks, including carbon monoxide poisoning from improperly operated generators and electrocution from downed power lines.

"In Florida, our history has been that we actually have as many people lose their lives after the storm and recovery," Fugate said on "Saturday in America."

"[There are] trees down, power lines, and just a variety of things. And be very careful as you start to clean up. We've seen people get injured from falls off ladders. We've seen carbon monoxide poisoning with people running their generators too close to their house. So, a lot of this can be prevented if people take their time," he added.

DREW BREES CALLS HURRICANE KATRINA 'DEFINING MOMENT' OF CAREER, CREDITS FAITH AND COMMUNITY FOR PERSEVERANCE

DeSantis said the state had strengthened its emergency response procedures after previous major hurricanes, helping crews deploy more quickly and better coordinate recovery efforts.

"I look back [at] Katrina in New Orleans and stuff, it just descended into chaos," DeSantis said.

"The folks that are on the ground both in our state agencies and in these local communities at the county level, they're very passionate about this project," DeSantis said, adding that crews had been working "around the clock."

"They will continue to do that until the situation is stabilized, but they do deserve a lot of credit. They're the best in the business," DeSantis said.

FOX Weather's Mike Rawlins contributed to this report.

item.title: Bill Maher mocks Mamdani for pivoting to Israel criticism in Oct. 7 tribute, calls it 'tone deaf'
item.description: Bill Maher blasted Zohran Mamdani's Oct. 7 anniversary statement on "Real Time," mocking the New York City mayor's pivot to criticizing Israel.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Bill Maher took aim at New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his statement marking the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attack on Israel.

Maher used Friday's episode of "Real Time" to criticize Mamdani's statement, in which the mayor called the day "profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers" and said the city grieves "alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss."

Mamdani went on to condemn the ongoing defensive acts being carried out by Israel, writing, "The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children."

ISRAEL AMB TORCHES MAMDANI OCT 7 POST: 'LIKE TURNING SEPTEMBER 11 INTO A DAY OF MOURNING FOR AL-QAEDA'
